newsitem.title: USA: Quaker Oats looks to put Snapple behind it.
newsitem.headline: Quaker Oats looks to put Snapple behind it.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co chairman William Smithburg, who is expected to retire within a year, said the company must put its failed Snapple acquisition behind it.
"Snapple clearly did not pan out," Smithburg said repeatedly at the annual shareholders meeting here Wednesday.
Asked if he wished Quaker had never bought Snapple, Smithburg simply said, "At this point in time (Quaker must) look forward."

Smithburg said he took responsibility for the due diligence and decision to buy Snapple about two years ago in a deal worth $1.8 billion, as well as the decision to sell it for $300 million. Coupled with $250 million in recouped taxes, the Snapple divestiture will bring in about $550 million.

Chicago-based Quaker Oats -- which has branded core businesses like Cap'n Crunch cereal, Rice a Roni side dish mixes and Gatorade sports drink -- took a $1.1 billion write-off for Snapple in the first quarter.
"The Snapple era is behind us," Smithburg told reporters after the meeting.
He said the sale of Snapple to Triarc Cos Inc is expected to be completed "soon," but did not give an exact timeframe.

Smithburg faced some criticism for Snapple at the otherwise low-keyed meeting. One shareholder demanded to see the "fairness" reports that were prepared by investment bankers when Snapple was purchased and later when it was sold.
The shareholder was later told that his request would be taken under advisement.

Smithburg, who in April announced plans to retire from Quaker, said he expected a successor to be named before the next annual meeting. The executive recruitment firm of SpencerStuart is "just getting underway" in a search for a new chief executive officer, he added.
Both internal and external candidates are being sought, Smithburg said, and added that executives outside the food industry would also be considered.
Smithburg has been chief executive officer at Quaker for 16 years, part of a 31-year career at the company.
Also at the annual meeting, a shareholder proposal asking the board to redeem the shareholder rights plan was narrowly defeated, with 44.3 percent of the votes cast in favor of the measure.
The proposal, made by the Amalgated Bank of New York Long View Collective Investment, sought the removal of the shareholder rights which, "could be used to entrench existing management."
The company opposed the measure, saying shareholder rights encourage acquiring parties to negotiate with the board.
